articles.title: New York City man shot in car with child present by ICE agents, mayor says
articles.summary: By Julia Harte and Kristina Cooke NEW YORK, Oct 8 (Reuters) - US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents shot and wounded a man on Thursday in his car wit...
articles.body:
Shooting involving US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the Bronx borough, in New York City

NEW YORK, Oct 8 (Reuters) - US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents shot and wounded a man on Thursday in his car with a child ‌present in the vehicle in the Bronx borough of New York City, according to ‌the mayor, city police and eyewitness accounts.

"Early reports indicate agents surrounded (the man) and a 5-year-old-child in his car before firing multiple ​rounds," New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement.

The mayor said the child was believed to have been physically unharmed. He referred to the man shot as a "New Yorker."

"This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation," Mamdani said, adding he had called President Donald Trump to talk about the incident. "When we speak ‌I will demand that he ends ⁠all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities."

ICE did not immediately respond to a request from ⁠Reuters for comment on the incident.

The incident was first reported on X by the New York Police Department, which gave few details other than to say: "there was a shooting involving federal law enforcement agents," and that ​the person ​shot was "currently conscious and receiving medical attention."

The shooting ​occurred at around 4 p.m. ET (2000 GMT) ‌in the Marble Hill neighborhood of the Bronx, the NYPD said.

An NYPD spokesperson said the agents involved in the shooting were part of DHS, the parent agency for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Customs and Border Protection and Border Patrol agencies, among others, and that federal authorities were investigating.

Pedro Almarez, owner of a nearby eatery, said he was working at the restaurant when he heard shots fired and ‌went outside to see several officers wearing ICE attire at ​the scene.

"There were a lot of ICE officers, three or ​four cars," Almarez told Reuters by phone, ​adding the man who was shot appeared to be between 20 and 30 ‌years of age. He said NYPD officers ​arrived about 10 minutes later.

The ​city police department said its officers were not involved in the shooting.

At the shooting scene, where police strung yellow crime-scene tape to cordon off a city block, a woman standing ​on a balcony overlooking the area ‌was heckling officers below about "taking our children."

(Reporting by Julia Harte in New York; Additional ​reporting by Jasper Ward in Washington; Writing and additional reporting by Steve Gorman in ​Los Angeles; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani and Chris Reese)

articles.title: Seca do rio Madeira dificulta acesso à água e à escola em RO | G1
articles.standfirst: Moradores relatam falta de água potável, prejuízos na produção de banana e dificuldades para chegar à escola. Estiagem afeta cerca de 22,9 mil pessoas em 85 localidades de Porto Velho.
articles.summary: A seca do rio Madeira fez Porto Velho decretar emergência após a estiagem afetar o acesso a água e escolas em 85 comunidades ribeirinhas de Rondônia.
articles.body:
A seca do rio Madeira mudou a rotina de quem vive às margens do curso d'água, em Porto Velho . Sem água potável e com dificuldades para se deslocar de barco, moradores enfrentam problemas para manter atividades que garantem a renda das famílias e até para chegar à escola.

🔎 A região Norte possui períodos regulares de estiagem, popularmente conhecidos como "verão amazônico", que ocorre entre julho e novembro. No entanto, monitoramentos feitos pelo SipamHidro, plataforma do Centro Gestor e Operacional do Sistema de Proteção da Amazônia (Censipam), mostram que o rio está mais de um metro abaixo do esperado para esta época do ano.

Na comunidade Bom Será, a presidente da associação local, Elizete Mota Leite, conta que os moradores não têm um poço próprio para abastecer a região. A única alternativa disponível atende apenas parte das famílias e, segundo ela, não fornece água potável.

"A gente se preocupa também de secar o nosso poço, o poço artesiano que a gente tem lá na beira da estrada. Meu esposo trabalha de cobrador, então ele leva o galão, traz um galão, só que aí pra nós somos seis, são quatro crianças e dois adultos, né, pra tu ver um galãozinho de água daquele é rapidinho, é rápido demais relatou.

A falta de água também afeta a produção agrícola. A agricultora Maria Rita conta que ficou quase quatro meses sem conseguir retirar a produção de banana do bananal. Sem condições de chegar ao local, parte dos frutos estragou antes de ser transportada.

"Já está estragando porque passou do tempo de tirar e quando não tem praia eu carrego na costa minha banana pra beira do rio, ponho na canoa, vou pro porto e subo lá com a banana. E agora no tempo da praia não dá pra fazer isso", disse.

Praias gigantes se formaram onde antes existia apenas água no rio Madeira , em Porto Velho. O cenário, causado pela estiagem, colocou a capital de Rondônia em situação de emergência. Segundo a prefeitura, cerca de 22,9 mil pessoas são afetadas pela seca em 85 localidades, incluindo áreas rurais, comunidades ribeirinhas e aldeias indígenas.

Na comunidade Brasileira, a agricultora Telma Temes da Silva, que nasceu e vive há 41 anos na região, diz que a paisagem mudou com o avanço da estiagem. Onde antes havia água, agora surgem bancos de areia e áreas de terra.

"O nosso rio passava aqui, hoje não é rio mais. Houve uma grande transformação, isso aqui era areia, hoje não é mais. Houve um grande soterramento do rio, tem 41 anos que moro aqui e o que eu posso ver com tudo isso é que daqui a um tempo vai acabar o nosso rio aqui", relatou.

A redução do nível do Madeira também afeta a rotina escolar da família. O filho de Telma estuda na comunidade de São Carlos e precisa caminhar vários quilômetros para chegar ao ponto de embarque do transporte fluvial.

“Meu filho estuda em São Carlos. Ele está enfrentando uma grande dificuldade, porque ele usa o transporte fluvial e para ele chegar até esse transporte fluvial, ele precisa caminhar de quatro a cinco a quilômetros a pé para poder chegar até o transporte", disse.

Porto Velho entra em estado de emergência

Na terça-feira (6), o rio marcou 2,62 metros, enquanto a média prevista para o período era de 3,9 metros, segundo dados do SipamHidro, plataforma do Centro Gestor e Operacional do Sistema de Proteção da Amazônia (Censipam).

A Prefeitura de Porto Velho decretou situação de emergência por 180 dias devido à estiagem . A medida foi classificada como desastre de nível II e permite solicitar apoio dos governos estadual e federal para o fornecimento de água potável por caminhões-pipa e embarcações, além de facilitar a contratação de serviços e a compra de materiais emergenciais.

O diretor executivo da Defesa Civil Municipal, Marcelo Duarte, afirmou que o fenômeno El Niño agravou a situação da estiagem neste ano.

“O El Ninõ, o efeito que a gente já está monitorando desde o começo do ano, ele agravou essa situação. Essa situação da estiagem é algo que ocorre todos os anos, mas esse ano ela foi agravada por conta do fenômeno e de todos os efeitos que dão ao redor dele”, explicou.

Com o nível baixo, bancos de areia e rochas dificultam a navegação. A Marinha restringiu a navegação noturna e houve redução no comboio de balsas de carga. O Departamento Nacional de Infraestrutura de Transportes (DNIT) prevê concluir os serviços de dragagem até novembro.

A Defesa Civil Municipal informou que as comunidades ribeirinhas devem receber assistência durante o período de estiagem.

articles.title: USS Lincoln returns to US after long deployment supporting war on Iran
articles.summary: Crew members express relief after a record 265 days at sea that strained conditions on board.
articles.body:
The United States aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has returned to its home port after a 322-day deployment, including a record 265 consecutive days at sea, during which it helped wage the US-Israel war on Iran.

The vessel returned to Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, California, on Thursday, where members of its crew were greeted by family and friends.

“It feels amazing,” 20-year-old Abel Ramirez told The Associated Press news agency, adding that his parents had driven from Texas to meet him. “There was a certain point when I never thought I would come off.”

The record-setting deployment of the USS Lincoln became a symbol for larger criticisms of the US war effort, which has dragged on since February with no clear end in sight and has strained US military stockpiles.

The prolonged deployment prompted a series of news reports calling attention to deteriorating conditions, food shortages and a series of reported suicide attempts by crew members.

Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth praised the sailors on Wednesday in remarks that accused the media of trying to turn the ship into “a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission”.

President Donald Trump and members of his administration have frequently lashed out at the news media for critical reporting on the war on Iran. Trump himself has called the reporting about the USS Lincoln “fake news”.

“The Lincoln has been out there for a period of time, a good period of time,” he said at an Oval Office meeting on August 17. “I know people on the Lincoln, and they say it’s beautifully maintained and beautifully taken care of.”

Earlier that month, when confronted with the amount of time the USS Lincoln had spent at sea without a port stop, Trump quipped that its deployment was “ not nearly long enough “.

The reports of mental health strain on the USS Lincoln come as public opinion polls show low approval ratings among US voters for the war against Iran.

On Thursday, the Pew Research Center released a poll that found 65 percent of Americans disapproved of Trump’s handling of the war, compared with 33 percent who approved.

The war has also fuelled concerns about the cost of living ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. Since the war began, Iran has hindered commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for the trade of fuel, fertiliser and other goods.

Sailors returning home on the USS Lincoln said that they were looking forward to fresh meals and spending time with their families.

Alma Solano Velez said that her husband, one of the US service members on board, shared a list of foods he had been craving over his 10-month deployment: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas, among others.

She added that he had spoken about “the lack of food and showers” and was looking forward to seeing their four-year-old daughter.

articles.title: Northern Ireland’s Sinn Fein faces police probe as protest tensions fester
articles.summary: The Democratic Unionist Party calls for the prosecution of Sinn Fein lawmakers who participated in the protest.
articles.body:
Northern Irish police have contacted representatives of Sinn Fein in an investigation into a protest that blocked a Protestant parade from marching through a Catholic area, the party said.

The Sinn Fein party leads Northern Ireland’s power-sharing government alongside its main pro-British rival, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), which has called for Sinn Fein lawmakers to be prosecuted.

In a statement posted to Facebook on Thursday, Sinn Fein confirmed “that a number of its representatives and party members received correspondence” from police.

“Sinn Fein will continue to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents who should be allowed to live in peace and free from sectarian intimidation,” the party said in the statement.

It added they have “stood with residents of the Garvaghy Road for the last two weeks in the face of provocation and the threat of an unwanted Orange march through their community”.

Northern Ireland’s High Court permitted the Protestant Orange Order to march on the Catholic Garvaghy Road for the first time in 28 years.

Police opened an investigation into what they called the unlawful protest of the march, and said people reasonably suspected of committing offences will receive letters for interviews.

Sinn Fein First Minister Michelle O’Neill and Sinn Fein President Mary Lou McDonald participated in the protests.

The DUP called for O’Neill and other lawmakers to be prosecuted.

“A political title is not a shield, and no one is above the law,” the party said in a statement on Thursday.

Before the Good Friday Agreement was signed, annual attempts by the Orange Order to march through the area triggered unrest across the British-run region until the route was banned in 1998.

The standoff has become a political crisis in Northern Ireland, affecting the region’s power-sharing government.

articles.title: Thousands protest in India’s Bengaluru as ‘Cockroach’ movement demands election chief resign
articles.summary: The demonstration came a day after police briefly detained opposition leader Rahul Gandhi at a New Delhi protest over the removal of over 130 million people from voter rolls.
articles.body: BENGALURU, India — Thousands of supporters of India’s youth “Cockroach” movement and several student groups demonstrated in the southern city of Bengaluru on Thursday, stepping up a nationwide campaign that is demanding the election chief’s resignation over a revision of voter lists that has removed over 130 million people from the rolls. The demonstration in Bengaluru came a day after opposition leader Rahul Gandhi was briefly detained by police at a protest in New Delhi. Dramatic images of police dragging Gandhi into a vehicle spread widely on social media, adding momentum to the protests calling for the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Gandhi’s Congress party and other opposition lawmakers also held protests in New Delhi on Thursday. The nationwide voter list review, known as the Special Intensive Revision, has been carried out in most of India’s states and federally administered territories. More than 130 million names have been removed so far, a number larger than the populations of countries like Japan and Mexico. Millions of people have appealed the deletions. The opposition says the removals have disproportionately affected voters who support them, while voters more likely to back Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s party have been preserved or added to the lists. The Election Commission and the government reject the allegations, saying the revision is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries. Those whose names have been struck off the list can appeal, but getting back on the rolls can be difficult. Critics say the requirements are confusing and some people may not have required documents such as older government records. The anger intensified last month following an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper that found two election commissioners had raised concerns about the process. The campaign has been led in part by the “Cockroach” movement, which began as an online youth campaign in May and has since organized street protests across the country. Its earlier nationwide demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of Modi’s education minister in July. Protesters are demanding Kumar’s resignation and an end to the removals, warning that they could disenfranchise millions more voters. The rallies pose a political challenge to Modi midway through his third term, as opposition parties seek to turn growing anger into a broader national campaign. Opposition leader Gandhi is also emerging as a prominent face of the protest. The “Cockroach” movement has called for more protests in New Delhi starting Saturday, with thousands expected to march to Jantar Mantar, the capital’s designated protest site. Police barricaded the area ahead of the demonstrations.

articles.title: Mamdani demands Trump release illegal immigrant shot by ICE agent as protests erupt in the Bronx
articles.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani demanded President Donald Trump release the man shot and injured by an ICE agent on Thursday in an incident that set off protests across New York City.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani demanded that President Donald Trump end all ICE enforcement in the state after a federal agent shot an illegal immigrant in the Bronx on Thursday, sparking protests and confrontations with law enforcement. At a news conference late Thursday night, Mamdani condemned the shooting and said he spoke with Trump for about two hours following the incident. Mamdani said he urged Trump to have the man released – an effort that was unsuccessful – and said New York City wants ICE agents out. "All they do is terrorize this city," the mayor said of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. ICE OFFICER SHOOTS, INJURES MAN DURING TARGETED IMMIGRATION OPERATION IN BRONX: DHS Mamdani also accused ICE of acting "with impunity" and spreading "chaos and terror" across the country, alleging that ICE has killed more people than it has saved. "Today's shooting is only further devastating confirmation of what we have long known," the mayor said. "ICE is rotten to its core," he added. Mamdani also confirmed that the man who was shot has been transported out of the hospital by ICE agents. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul also said she spoke to Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. "Tonight, I spoke with President Trump and DHS Secretary Mullin about the shooting in Marble Hill," she said on X. "I expressed outrage on behalf of New Yorkers and urged them to halt ICE enforcement operations in New York. I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public so we can establish the facts and get to the truth." ICE SHOOTING ROCKS AUSTIN AS DEMOCRAT DEMANDS BODYCAM VIDEO, INDEPENDENT PROBE ICE was attempting to arrest a wanted man from the Dominican Republic at around 4 p.m. on Thursday when an agent opened fire and wounded him, according to DHS, which did not provide details on what led to the shooting. "ICE officers immediately rendered aid. The individual is alive and at a local hospital. The FBI and HSI are on the scene. The incident remains under investigation. More information will be shared as it becomes available," DHS said in a statement. DHS said the man, who was described as an illegal immigrant, had a prior grand larceny conviction and previous arrests involving assault, robbery, drug possession and weapons possession. The agency also alleged that he had ties to the Trinitarios gang. Later Thursday night, New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch identified the man as a 28-year-old and said a 5-year-old boy believed to be his son was inside the vehicle with him during the shooting. "Based on evidence collected at the scene, we know that at least one ICE agent discharged the seven rounds, striking the driver in the neck below his left ear," Tisch said, adding that the boy was not injured and is in the care of a family member. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The agency said the man was arrested by New York City police on Dec. 7, 2023, but was released several days later. DHS blamed New York City's sanctuary policies for his release. Hundreds of demonstrators gathered outside NewYork-Presbyterian Allen Hospital, where the wounded man was being treated, and chanting "ICE off our streets" and "No justice, no peace." Protesters and police were seen shoving one another during the demonstration as officers began to set barricades, and some demonstrators threw water bottles at the officers. "From Palestine to Mexico, all these walls have got to go," the group chanted. Police made some arrests during the demonstration. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Photos: Gaza before and after – a city transformed by war
articles.summary: Archive and recent photos show how three years of war left Gaza’s streets, landmarks and public spaces unrecognisable.
articles.body:
Gaza City – More than 80 percent of Gaza’s buildings have been damaged or destroyed since Israel launched its war on the besieged enclave in October 2023, according to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, turning whole neighbourhoods into rubble and wiping out much of its infrastructure.

For generations, Gaza’s streets, markets, schools, hospitals and public spaces formed the backdrop to everyday life. They were places where people worked, studied, shopped, met friends and family, and built memories.

Many of the city’s familiar landmarks also carried a much longer history, reflecting Gaza’s thousands of years as a crossroads of different civilisations.

The war has also changed the face of Gaza by damaging or destroying many of those historic and recognisable landmarks.

UNESCO has verified damage to 164 cultural sites since October 2023, including 128 buildings of historical or artistic interest, 14 religious sites, nine monuments, eight archaeological sites, two museums and three depositories of movable cultural property.

Among them are the Great Omari Mosque, Gaza’s oldest mosque, Qasr al-Basha, the ancient Samaritan Bathhouse, al-Qissariya Market and the Church of Saint Porphyrius complex.

Some of these places have been reduced to ruins, while others remain standing but heavily damaged. The destruction has altered not only individual buildings but the streets and neighbourhoods around them, removing landmarks that once helped people recognise and navigate their city.

This photo series contrasts archive images of some of Gaza’s most recognisable streets, markets and public buildings with new photographs taken three years into the war, showing how these familiar places have changed after years of bombardment and destruction.

images.caption: Gaza's historic landmarks have been reduced to rubble, altering the city's landscape and erasing generations of memories. [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera]

Gaza's port has long been a central part of life along the city's coast, serving as a base for local fishermen and a familiar gathering place for residents. After three years of war, the port and its surrounding coastline have been heavily damaged, with thousands of displaced families now sheltering in tents across the port area. [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera]

Al-Rashid Street, Gaza's main coastal road, stretches along the Mediterranean and was once a popular destination lined with cafes, restaurants, shops and hotels. After three years of war, much of the area has been damaged or destroyed, with tents now filling parts of the coastline. [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera]

Rashad al-Shawwa Cultural Centre in Gaza City's Remal neighbourhood was a landmark cultural venue, hosting exhibitions, conferences and public events. Three years of war have left the centre heavily damaged, with parts of the building destroyed and the surrounding area in ruins. [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera]

Qasr al-Basha, a 13th-century Mamluk palace in Gaza's Old City, was restored and turned into an archaeological museum in 2010. Once one of Gaza's best-preserved historic landmarks, the palace has been heavily damaged after three years of war. [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera]

Al-Hasayna Mosque, also known as al-Mina Mosque, stood beside Gaza's port and was inaugurated in 2017, becoming a familiar landmark on the city's shoreline. The mosque was completely destroyed in November 2023. [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera]

articles.title: J.K. Rowling’s Wizarding World expands: Bloomsbury officially announces two new Harry Potter Pocket Potters books on Minerva McGonagall and Fred & George Weasley for February 2027 release
articles.summary: Harry Potter fans have already had a busy year full of new ways to revisit the stories they love.
articles.body: Harry Potter fans have already had a busy year full of new ways to revisit the stories they love. The critically acclaimed Audible Full-Cast Audio Editions gave listeners months of enjoyment and roughly a hundred hours of fresh performances. At the same time, the first trailer for the upcoming HBO series arrived, building anticipation for its Christmas premiere.Now, ahead of that television adaptation, Bloomsbury Publishing is officially expanding the Pocket Potters line with two new books due in February 2027. These titles centre on three of Harry’s closest allies: Minerva McGonagall and the Weasley twins, Fred and George. Aimed primarily at younger readers, the books are also the kind of colourful, collectible releases that longtime fans who already own more Harry Potter merchandise than they need will still find hard to resist.Two new guides to familiar facesPocket Potters: Fred and George, illustrated by Helen Brady, follows Hogwarts’ favourite troublemaking twins from their years of causing chaos at school to the creation of Weasleys’ Wizard Wheezes. The book will explore their best pranks and inventions, their talent for getting around the rules, and the spectacular decision to leave Hogwarts before opening their joke shop in Diagon Alley. Readers can expect plenty of references to Puking Pastilles, Extendable Ears, and other products that probably should never have been allowed near a classroom. The twins’ energy and inventiveness have always stood out, and this volume gives those qualities a focused, illustrated stage.Pocket Potters: McGonagall, illustrated by Natalie Smillie, turns attention to the formidable Hogwarts professor. It will explore her role as Head of Gryffindor House, her ability to transform into a tabby cat, and the Transfiguration lessons that generations of students learned never to arrive late for. The book also looks at McGonagall’s relationship with Harry and her fellow professors, her fierce loyalty to Hogwarts, and the dry sense of humour that often hid beneath that pointed hat. Together the two titles bring supporting characters into sharper focus without rewriting the larger story.A growing collection of pocket-sized storiesThese new releases join the existing Pocket Potters books already available for Harry Potter, Ron Weasley, Hermione Granger, Professor Dumbledore, and Luna Lovegood. Each volume is packed with quotes, key story moments, illustrations, and small facts designed to introduce young readers to the Wizarding World in a bright and approachable way. The format remains consistent across the series: short enough to read in one sitting, yet detailed enough to feel like a proper keepsake. For children just discovering the books, they offer an easy entry point. For adults who grew up with the original novels, they provide a compact and colourful way to revisit favourite characters.Timing that fits a larger revivalThe February 2027 publication date arrives only a few months after the HBO series is scheduled to begin. With the Audible editions already giving fans a new audio experience and the television adaptation preparing to introduce the story to another generation, the Pocket Potters expansions keep the printed side of the franchise moving forward as well. Bloomsbury’s choice to highlight McGonagall and the Weasley twins rather than the central trio suggests quiet confidence that these supporting figures still have stories worth telling on their own. For readers who first met them years ago, the books offer a compact return to familiar ground. For those just starting out, they provide another gentle doorway into a world that continues to grow.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Nobel Peace Prize 2026 goes to Navi Pillay
articles.summary: A total of 208 individuals and 79 organizations were nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize, which President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed he deserves to win. Follow for live updates.
articles.body:
• The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize goes to South African jurist and human rights pioneer Navi Pillay “for her efforts to promote peace and international law.”

• US President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed he deserves the peace prize , saying this week that it “would be a great discredit” to the Nobel committee if it does not select him for the honor.

• Nobel Prizes in medicine , physics , chemistry and literature were also annnounced this week.

The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

We’re about to find out the winner of this year’s Nobel Peace Prize. The committee have entered the room and will shortly begin their announcement.

The peace prize takes on a different significance in a time when there is so much instability.

Destructive wars continued around the globe last year. Russia’s war in Ukraine shows no signs of ending soon, more than a thousand Palestinians have been killed by Israeli strikes in Gaza even after a fragile ceasefire came into effect last November, civil war in Sudan is still raging, and war in Iran has further destabilized the Middle East.

The peace prize “highlights the urgency of certain causes and certain challenges,” said Karim Haggag, the director of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).

As well as these wars, global military spending rose by almost 3% last year, fueled mostly by ballooning defense budgets in Europe and Asia, SIPRI found in their annual report.

The ICC and ICJ are two institutions that experts have highlighted as potential recipients of the award this year.

The Nobel committee can send different messages depending on who they choose to award. If human rights activists or journalists are recognized, the message could be one of “setting an example of moral courage in the face of very strong political or authoritarian pressure,” Haggag added.

If there is no “suitable” candidate for the peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee can choose not to award it.

The process for selecting Nobel peace laureates closely follows the will of Alfred Nobel , the Swedish chemist who gave his fortune to establish the prizes. His will says the award will be given to “the person who shall have done the most or the best work for fraternity between nations and the abolition or reduction of standing armies and the formation and spreading of peace congresses.”

The Nobel Foundation’s bylaws say that “if none of the works under consideration is found to be of the importance indicated in the first paragraph, the prize money shall be reserved until the following year.”

In the past, the committee has chosen to abstain 19 times – most notably during the first and second world wars – but the peace prize has been awarded every year since 1971.

Some observers have argued that withholding the prize could send a strong message that the world must step up its peacebuilding efforts. But scholars of conflict and disarmament have previously told CNN that withholding the prize could send a message of resignation and hopelessness.

Another potential laureate featured on the list released by the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO) is the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), a US-based watchdog organization that promotes press freedom by defending the right of media workers to report safely and without fear of reprisal. It also advocates for the release of detained and imprisoned journalists.

CPJ also tracks the killing, detention and targeting of journalists worldwide. The organization said there were a record-high number of journalists killed in 2024 and 2025.

As of December 2025, CPJ researchers have documented 335 journalists worldwide who are imprisoned and 85 who are missing. The watchdog also found that 130 journalists and media workers were killed last year.

“Beyond active warzones, journalists face lethal risks from organized crime and systematic repression,” the PRIO said in a statement. “From targeted killings in armed conflicts and by criminal networks, to the relentless harassment and suppression of independent media in countries such as Russia, Mexico, Myanmar and Afghanistan, reporting truth has increasingly become a matter of life and death.”

More than three years after it broke out, Sudan’s deadly civil war is still raging, fueling one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises .

More than 150,000 people have been killed , 14 million more displaced and 33.7 million people – more than two-thirds of Sudan’s population – require urgent humanitarian assistance, the Red Cross reported in July.

But international aid organizations have struggled to reach those in need. In their absence, the community-led Emergency Response Rooms have stepped in, providing food, clean water, medication, community kitchens, health clinics and trauma counseling.

The network of community-led initiatives is listed as a possible laureate by the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO), which publishes a list of five worthy potential winners each year.

“In light of Ukraine and Iran and all of these big geopolitical wars, the Sudan war can end up a little on the back bench, but it is a war that entangles in it a lot of the dynamics in the Middle East with the rising conflict over the Red Sea,” says Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the PRIO.

Alsanosi Adam, a volunteer and one of the Emergency Response Rooms’ spokespeople, told the Guardian last year: “You risk anything from intimidation to death. From torture to being killed – and everything in between.”

The network emerged from the Sudanese tradition of “Nafeer,” meaning a “collective call to action,” and first developed during earlier upheaval in 2018 and the Covid-19 pandemic, according to aid group Save the Children.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ) are the two main courts of global law, and frequently appear on the shortlist of potential Nobel Peace Prize winners listed by the Peace Research Institute Oslo.

They have received unprecedented international attention for their efforts to prosecute alleged war crimes committed in Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and Israel’s war in Gaza.

The ICJ, which prosecutes states, has ordered Israel to “take all measures” to prevent genocide in Gaza after South Africa accused Israel of violating international laws on genocide in its war in the territory.

The ICC, which prosecutes individuals, issued an arrest warrant in March 2023 for Russian President Vladimir Putin and another Russian official for an alleged scheme to deport Ukrainian children. It issued arrest warrants for Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defense minister, Yoav Gallant, in 2024.

But picking the ICC could invoke the wrath of the Trump administration, which targeted several ICC prosecutors with sanctions after it issued the warrants for Israeli officials, as part of its campaign to “dismantle” the court — an effort condemned by Europe and Japan. Neither the US nor Israel are party to the ICC.

“We do feel pressure but as I’ve said the dedication of our staff is extraordinary and they continue to do their work.”

For the last 26 years, the International Space Station (ISS) has been continuously occupied by humans orbiting the Earth, becoming an increasingly rare example of international cooperation.

“Giving the prize to the ISS would be one way of celebrating what we can achieve as humanity when we are able to cooperate,” said Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, which compiles a widely respected shortlist of potential Nobel Peace Prize nominees.

Cooperation on the ISS is enabled through the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which also prohibited countries from placing nuclear weapons or installing military bases in outer space, Gjerløw points out.

But that treaty does not prohibit the use of conventional weapons in space, and the US military recently confirmed it had deployed weapons in orbit.

So, highlighting the ISS “could also give an impetus for politicians internationally to improve on the Outer Space Treaty,” or establish a new space station that also includes China when the current one is decommissioned in 2030, Gjerløw told CNN.

Jointly run by NASA and its equivalent agencies in Russia, Japan, Canada and Europe, the ISS represents “the most politically complex space exploration program ever undertaken,” according to NASA’s website.

Research there has advanced our understanding in many areas of science, including drug development, quantum mechanics and black holes.

Predicting the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize is notoriously difficult, with the nominees only made public 50 years after it’s awarded. But every year, the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO) compiles a widely respected shortlist of potential candidates.

The humanitarian organization Save the Children and Mykola Kuleba, who founded Save Ukraine to advocate for children affected by war in the eastern European country, are on the PRIO’s director’s list this year.

Save the Children works in conflict zones – notably in Gaza, Sudan, Ukraine, Myanmar and the DRC – to provide humanitarian support and help children continue their education.

Save Ukraine , meanwhile, works to rescue abducted children in Russia and Russian-occupied territories.

“We don’t work with the Russian authorities or any officials in occupied territories, because it’s really dangerous.

In 2024, about 19% of the world’s children lived in a conflict zone, double the proportion from 30 years ago, according to figures from the UN children’s agency (UNICEF).

CNN’s Ivana Kottasová contributed reporting.

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize last year after being forced into hiding following a disputed 2024 election in her country.

Machado won the prize for her “struggle to achieve a just and peaceful transition from dictatorship to democracy,” the Nobel committee said.

Her recognition came at an extremely volatile time for Venezuela as the Trump administration intensified its pressure campaign against the country, which culminated in US special forces raiding the capital Caracas and capturing then-President Nicolás Maduro in January.

Machado sought to use the Nobel prize, which US President Donald Trump has publicly coveted, to ally herself with him. She dedicated her award to him in October last year, telling CNN’s Christiane Amanpour that it was “absolutely fair, and that’s what the Venezuelan people feel.”

After US forces toppled Maduro, Machado even traveled to the White House and presented Trump with her medal. The Nobel committee has said the award is not transferable.

However, Machado has been largely sidelined from any role in a post-Maduro government. The Trump administration has instead dealt with acting President Delcy Rodríguez, who previously served as Maduro’s oil minister and vice president . And Machado has been unable to re-enter Venezuela after traveling to Norway in December to collect her medal.

Deciding who will be the recipient of a Nobel Prize is a secretive process. This year, the Norwegian Nobel Committee has selected its peace prize laureates from a pool of nominees, comprising 208 individuals and 79 organizations.

The nominations process starts in September each year. Academics, Nobel laureates and lawmakers from around the world had until January 31 to submit nominations.

The five-member committee then whittles that down to a closely guarded shortlist of 20 to 30 candidates.

During the evaluation process, the committee may add further names to the list. Information on the nominees and nominators is not disclosed for 50 years.

The committee members, who are appointed by the Norwegian parliament, also consults their advisers, normally Norwegian professors with expertise in related areas .

The committee only reaches a decision in its last meeting right before the announcement of the award, typically aiming for a unanimous vote.

The committee will “always revert to the will of Alfred Nobel,” which contains the three criteria of “promoting peace, disarmament and international cooperation,” according to Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO).

“There are different topics… but it always needs to connect them back to the testament of Nobel,” he said.

US President Donald Trump has expressed his desire to win a Nobel Peace Prize at almost every opportunity — including in the Oval Office this week.

Trump said not awarding him the prize “would be a great discredit” to the selecting committee. The president again said he’d “settled eight wars” while in office, a claim CNN’s Fact Check team describes as an exaggeration.

But experts say it is unlikely he will win. “It’s very difficult to see how the ideals of the Nobel Peace Prize committee would align with the actual policies and positions adopted by the president,” said Karim Haggag, the director of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

Nominations for the award closed on January 31, meaning the prize often relates to the previous year. In 2025, a Trump administration-brokered ceasefire came into force in Gaza, though it remains fragile and Israeli strikes have killed over 1,000 Palestinians since. Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have attempted to negotiate a peace deal to end Russia’s war in Ukraine but have not yet reached any breakthroughs.

Last year too, Trump threatened to seize Greenland and US forces raided a complex in Venezuela to capture then-president Nicolas Maduro .

The committee still considers events after January 31 as part of the evaluation of nominees, during which time the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran, killing thousands in Iran and Lebanon, and sparking months of instability in the Middle East.

The Nobel Prizes were established in the last will and testament of Swedish industrialist and chemist Alfred Nobel, best known for his invention of dynamite.

Prizes are bestowed on individuals for their incredible accomplishments in five categories – physiology or medicine, chemistry, physics, literature and peace – a reflection of Nobel’s interests.

Nobel stipulated in his will that his fortune was to be used to honor “those who, during the preceding year, shall have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind.”

Additionally, in 1968, Sweden’s central bank created a new prize – the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel.

Welcome to our live coverage of the announcement of this year’s Nobel Peace Prize. The Norwegian Nobel Committee have sifted through 287 nominations for this year’s prize and we’ll soon learn the winner.

The laureate will be announced at the Norwegian Nobel Institute at 11 a.m. local time (5 a.m. ET).

The award ceremony will take place in Oslo, Norway on December 10 — the anniversary of the death of Alfred Nobel, the Swedish chemist, engineer and industrialist who created the prize.

articles.title: Neha Bora: India's feisty Gen Z protester who is taking on Modi
articles.summary: Neha Bora has emerged as one of the most recognisable faces from India's recent Gen Z-led protests.
articles.body:
When India's Gen Z-led protesters return to Delhi this weekend for demonstrations seeking the resignation of the country's top election official, one of the prominent faces at the forefront will be that of a 29-year-old PhD student.

Neha Bora is a theatre artist and activist who has been with the All India Students' Association (Aisa), a Left-wing organisation known for campus politics, for the past decade and been its president for the past two years.

But Neha's - who uses "they" and "them" as personal pronouns - visibility is no longer limited to campuses.

Viral videos over the past few days show them being dragged through the street by a group of female police officials, climbing on top of police barricades, raising their fist and shouting slogans, and being detained.

Photos of them smiling while being carried away by policewomen have also gone viral.

In a recent BBC Bangla interview, Neha played down the attention they've been receiving.

"I know it happened in front of the camera so it seems like it's something different," they said. "But I have seen all student activists with the Left doing the same things that I have been doing. It's just that there is a camera on me, so people think something different is happening."

The attention on Neha comes at a time when several high-profile protests are being held on India's streets in what is being seen as one of the biggest challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 12 years in power.

There's the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a Gen Z-led online satirical movement - that held weeks-long protests in Delhi in the summer over education reforms. It ended in July only after education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.

Separately, some of India's opposition parties, especially the Congress, have also taken to the streets over electoral reforms. For the past few days, videos of Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra being shoved and jostled and detained have gone viral and made headlines in India.

Saturday's protest in Delhi has been called by the CJP, which is seeking the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating electoral rolls to favour Modi's BJP. Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the accusation.

Although not a member of the CJP, Neha has said their group would also participate.

Born in the northern state of Uttarakhand, Neha lived in different cities as a child as their army officer father moved for his postings.

After graduating from Delhi University, they did a master's degree from Ambedkar University in the capital and are now a PhD student at the prestigious Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU).

Neha first came into the spotlight in the summer during the CJP's protest over education reforms.

Neha and Aisa were at the protest from the start, but not many knew them at that point. That changed after 28 June, when educationist and scientist Sonam Wangchuk began a hunger strike in CJP's support and Neha and a few others from Aisa also joined him.

"It was an obvious choice for us. We've been protesting against paper leaks and education reforms for a long time," Neha later said in an interview.

While most of the attention was focused on Wangchuk, whose reputation and presence galvanised the movement, Neha's outspokenness and combative speeches began to get them noticed.

After Wangchuk and others were moved to hospital , Neha continued fasting despite having lost 8kg.

Even after being moved to hospital, they said in a video: "The fight continues. Once I've recovered, we'll meet you again on the streets to continue our fight for our right."

After the protests ended in July, Neha has established themselves as a Gen Z leader who's courted by the CJP and media, besides appearing alongside Rahul Gandhi at press conferences.

But Neha's involvement with Aisa and leftist politics and statements criticising PM Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and other BJP leaders have also led to "lots of disagreements with my family as my parents are staunch supporters of BJP".

And last month, at least three police complaints were lodged in Uttar Pradesh state by BJP against Neha for making "objectionable remarks" against the chief minister - they came two days after Aisa's police complaint that Neha had received death threats .

Neha, who has been travelling to many Indian cities to participate in protests in support of students, also made headlines when a man allegedly threw ink at them during a protest march in Jharkhand state. A photo Neha shared on Instagram showed their face streaked with ink stains. Police said they had detained the man.

The noisy protests and repeated detentions have earned Neha a reputation for being a street fighter.

"The streets have always dictated the course of politics in this country and they will continue to do so, more so in the coming few years," they told BBC Bangla.

"If we look at the social changes of the recent past, those social changes did not come from people sitting in parliament; they came from the streets," they said.

Now as the authorities gear up for 10 October's protest at Jantar Mantar against CEC Kumar, Neha and Aisa have said they would be back in the streets with the CJP to "protect democracy".

articles.title: Prison riot in Mexico’s Sinaloa state kills 10 and leaves 16 injured
articles.summary: A deadly riot broke out during family visiting hours Thursday at a prison in the state of Sinaloa in northwestern Mexico, state authorities said.
articles.body: MEXICO CITY — A deadly riot broke out during family visiting hours Thursday at a prison in the state of Sinaloa in northwestern Mexico, state authorities said. The violence occurred Thursday morning at the El Castillo Penitentiary in the port city of Mazatlan. Sinaloa’s Public Security Secretariat said on X that nine inmates and one family member were killed in the incident, while 16 prisoners were taken for medical treatment after being injured. Local media reported that inmates used firearms during the fight. Authorities have not yet said how the deaths occurred. Following the clash, members of the army, National Guard, navy and state security forces entered the prison to restore order. Mexico’s federal security cabinet said the prison, which houses 1,800 inmates, is now “under control.” Overcrowding, driven in part by the use of pretrial detention — which keeps thousands of prisoners behind bars without a sentence — combined with insufficient prison staff, has fueled corruption and violence inside prisons, according to analysts. Last May, a riot broke out at a prison in Culiacan, the capital of Sinaloa, leaving seven inmates dead and another injured. Mexico has 276 prisons, including 14 federal penitentiaries and 249 state prisons. The prison population reached 261,388 people as of February, according to official figures. Violence erupted in Sinaloa in September 2024 amid an internal power struggle between two factions of the Sinaloa Cartel, pitting the sons of convicted former drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, known as “Los Chapitos,” against followers of another detained former cartel leader, Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada. The Thursday riot comes as Mexico’s government faces pressure from the Trump administration to crack down on cartels.

articles.title: Three years after October 7, prolonged war takes its toll on Israelis
articles.summary: Children’s psychiatric emergency visits have more than doubled in Israel, study shows.
articles.body:
As Israel marks the third anniversary of the 7 October Hamas-led attacks, the psychological toll on its society remains visible, with an increase in PTSD among children, more adults struggling with everyday life amid mental health issues, and a rise in suicides among soldiers, experts have told Al Jazeera.

About 1,200 people died in the attacks on villages and army outposts in southern Israel, while Israel’s assault on Gaza has since killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. Gaza has been left almost uninhabitable amid a wave of destruction that a UN commission of inquiry has concluded amounts to genocide. Meanwhile, Israeli society continues to function, but beneath the surface, the attacks, war and missile strikes have compounded the psychological strain among its people.

New research has found that one in five Israelis reports severe difficulties with daily functioning because of their mental health, according to the National Mental Health Barometer, conducted by Clalit Health Services’ Research Institute and the Myers-JDC-Brookdale Institute.

Among children and adolescents, separate Clalit research shared with Al Jazeera recorded a 121 per cent increase in psychiatric emergency visits compared with the period before the war. Behind those figures are families living with bereavement and fears about what comes next.

During a webinar for journalists organised by Clalit Health Services to mark the anniversary, Irit Ben Arye recounted how her husband, Haim Ben Arye, drove south to help evacuate survivors from Kibbutz Be’eri. It was one of the communities attacked by Palestinian fighters on 7 October 2023.

The 52-year-old bus driver returned home crying, she says. About two weeks later, he died by suicide.

The couple were married for 30 years and had eight children. Irit worries about the lasting effects on them. Recounting to journalists what she told her children following the death of her husband, she said: “You have to ask for help, if something is bothering you, if you’re in pain, in the dark, you feel that you are alone.”

“Cry, ask, break something. Make yourself noticed, make us notice that you are in pain.”

The Ben Arye family are not the only ones experiencing mental distress. In fact, one-third of the Israeli population felt they needed mental health treatment, according to the National Mental Health Barometer report. Half reported that their leisure activities had been affected, while 35 per cent said they had difficulty forming and maintaining close relationships.

Israel’s attacks on Iran and retaliatory missile strikes have brought further periods of fear and interruption to civilian life. With missiles and airstrikes raining down on Israel at various times since 7 October, everyday activities can become calculations about access to shelter and the possibility of another attack.

Eric Vermetten, a professor of psychiatry at Leiden University Medical Center in the Netherlands, told Al Jazeera that this type of repeated exposure to danger can lead to long-lasting psychological issues. “Repeated attacks, warning sirens and displacement turn ordinary decisions – where to sleep, whether to send children to school, how to plan tomorrow – into questions of safety,” he said.

“Maintaining that vigilance is exhausting: sleep becomes deeply fragmented, concentration falters and anxiety, irritability or withdrawal can seriously strain relationships,” he added.

Drawing on records from about five million members, Clalit Health Services’ assessment has found that psychiatric emergency visits among children and teenagers more than doubled over this period.

Edgar Jones, professor at King’s College London’s Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience, told Al Jazeera that people respond differently to prolonged conflict. Some do adapt and develop ways of coping.

But if people experience the destruction of their home or the death of a relative, they may develop post-traumatic illness or depression, he said. “Many of those in this group will become war-weary should their daily lives continue to be disrupted and threatened.”

“Everyone has a breaking point,” Jones said.

The effects of prolonged warfare are also apparent among those carrying out Israel’s military attacks. Soldiers, including young conscripts, have been deployed to Gaza, where a United Nations commission of inquiry concluded that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians.

“For reservists, moving repeatedly between combat and civilian life may leave little to no time to reconnect with family or make sense of their experiences – loss, guilt, shame, anger, despair – before returning to duty,” Vermetten said.

Jones added: “They may, when reflecting on what they have been ordered to do, or failed to do, experience moral injury”.

“This arises when their actions challenge their view of themselves, sometimes leading to guilt, shame and anger against themselves.”

Israeli parliamentary data recorded 279 suicide attempts among serving soldiers between January 2024 and July 2025. Combat soldiers accounted for 78 per cent of military suicide deaths in 2024. The figures exclude veterans who died by suicide after leaving service.

Vermetten cautioned against treating suicide as an inevitable consequence of prolonged war, but said that “conflict, loss and isolation can increase vulnerability” among soldiers who go on to take their own lives.

The psychological consequences of Israel’s military campaigns extend far beyond its own population. Since 7 October 2023, its assaults on Gaza and Lebanon, as well as attacks on Iran have brought death, destruction and displacement across the region, leaving children particularly vulnerable to lasting trauma.

UNICEF estimated that in Lebanon, 770,000 children have experienced psychological distress, while almost two-thirds of households reported that their children were anxious or nervous. The conflict has also compounded years of economic crisis, leaving families struggling to meet basic needs as well as support their children.

In Gaza, the scale of destruction and displacement has eroded the foundations on which psychological recovery depends , with hospitals and homes destroyed across the enclave.

UNICEF estimates that more than one million children are in need of mental health and psychosocial support, while much of the population is suffering from hunger, amid bombardment that has continued despite a so-called “ceasefire” last October.

“Children know trauma does not end when the bombing stops,” Jonathan Crickx, UNICEF’s chief of communication in the State of Palestine, said in February.

articles.title: Look of the Week: Who wears short shorts? Juergen Teller
articles.summary: You may have an idea as to what fashion people wear to runway shows. Then the avant-garde photographer proves you wrong.
articles.body: You might have an idea as to what fashion people wear to runway shows. Then photographer Juergen Teller shows up, as always, to prove you wrong. Even amid the hooplah of peacocking influencers and frazzled fashion editors, Teller’s flash of Ibiza club-colored sportswear demanded a double take. He wore them a number of times throughout Paris Fashion Week, including to the Schiaparelli show, in a café across the way from the Eiffel Tower not far from the Commes des Garcon catwalk, and most recently at the opening of the Tate’s latest exhibition, “The ‘90s: Art and Fashion,” in London. In fact, he’s been wearing a version of these shorts since 2004. Many people in fashion extol the virtues of a ‘uniform.’ Designers in particular will often take their catwalk bow in clothes radically different from the ones they’ve spent the last 15 minutes convincing you to buy. Take Jonathan Anderson’s blue jeans, Salomon shoes and crewneck sweaters for example, or Carolina Herrera’s crisp white button-down tucked into an A-line skirt. “I spend all my time thinking about what everyone else is wearing, so the last thing I want to do is spend too much time thinking about what I put on,” Michael Kors told Time Magazine of his signature jeans, aviators, sneakers and black T-shirt formula in 2016. Getting dressed takes up sacred time, and time is money — especially for fashion folk. But while most embrace an inoffensive, fly-under-the-radar outfit, Teller, an image-making pariah, unsurprisingly takes a different approach. In his photography work, he’s recently been able to puncture fashion’s bubble with flat, fabulously ironic celebrity portraits that reject the conventional glossy magazine spread, and asks bravely: Why do we need another in-studio photoshoot with Natalie Portman in a Dior gown when we could see her amidst the chaos of a Hollywood tourist merch shop? The way Teller packages himself is the same. He repeatedly pairs his Stabilo-hued shorts cut high on the thigh (“What’s the point of shorts if they’re not short?” He once told the Financial Times) with ASICS sneakers worn with ankle socks as if he’s fresh off a jog round the park. It’s a head-to-toe snub of the unwritten dress codes in an industry that cashes in on insecurity and appearances. That is his first flex. The second is that these trademark briefs are reportedly custom-made Celine — a tongue-in-cheek gift from his close friend Phoebe Philo during her tenure — and so they get the fashion seal of approval anyway.
